nameStory: The princess tree gets its regal name from its showy purple flowers that bloom in spectacular clusters, fit for royalty. It's also called the empress tree, honoring Anna Pavlovna, a Russian princess who became Queen of the Netherlands. The scientific name Paulownia also commemorates this same royal figure.
description: The princess tree is a fast-growing deciduous tree that can reach 30-40 feet tall with a broad, spreading crown. It's easily recognized by its enormous heart-shaped leaves that can grow as large as dinner plates, and its striking clusters of purple, trumpet-shaped flowers that appear in spring. Originally from China, this tree has escaped cultivation and spread throughout much of New England, though it's considered an invasive species.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Huge heart-shaped leaves, often 6-12 inches across, with a soft fuzzy texture on the undersides that feels like velvet when you touch it. They're arranged opposite each other on branches.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Showy purple trumpet-shaped flowers about 2 inches long, clustered in upright spikes that smell sweetly fragrant. They bloom in late spring before the leaves fully emerge.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Oval woody capsules about 1-2 inches long that split open to release thousands of tiny winged seeds. The empty capsules often persist through winter.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth grayish bark on younger trees that becomes slightly furrowed with age. The bark remains relatively thin and light-colored even on mature trees.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Extremely fast-growing with thick, somewhat brittle branches that spread to form a broad, open crown. Often multi-trunked when growing in the wild.

habitat: Princess trees thrive in disturbed areas like roadsides, forest edges, abandoned lots, and along railroad tracks throughout New England. They prefer well-drained soils and full sun but are quite adaptable to various soil types. You'll often spot them growing as escaped ornamentals near old home sites or in areas where fill dirt has been moved around.

seasonality.spring: Purple flower clusters bloom dramatically in May before the leaves emerge, making them highly visible. The enormous heart-shaped leaves unfurl after flowering and grow rapidly.
seasonality.summer: Huge green leaves dominate the appearance, creating dense shade. Woody seed capsules begin forming and the tree grows vigorously with new shoots often appearing from the base.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow-green to brown before dropping, and the woody seed capsules ripen and split open. The tree often loses leaves earlier than many native species.
seasonality.winter: Distinctive woody seed capsules persist on bare branches, and large flower buds for next year are visible as fuzzy brown clusters at branch tips.

funFact: A single princess tree can produce up to 20 million tiny seeds per year, and these seeds are so light and numerous that they can travel over 100 miles on the wind - which is why you might find princess trees growing in the most unexpected places, far from the nearest parent tree!
confusionNotes: The enormous heart-shaped leaves might be confused with catalpa trees, but catalpa leaves are arranged in groups of three (whorled) rather than opposite pairs, and catalpa flowers are white with spots rather than solid purple. Remember: princess trees have purple flowers and opposite leaves, catalpas have white spotted flowers and whorled leaves.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its beautiful flowers, the princess tree is considered an invasive species in New England and can crowd out native plants. It's sometimes called the foxglove tree because its flowers resemble those of foxglove plants, though it's not closely related to the herb foxglove.
compareHints: Princess tree is the only Paulownia species commonly found in New England. Among fast-growing non-native trees, it's most similar to catalpa, but princess tree has opposite heart-shaped leaves and purple flowers, while catalpa has whorled leaves and white flowers with purple spots. The princess tree's velvet-soft leaf undersides are also distinctive compared to catalpa's smooth leaves.
